description: ​We are "OrbitLogic", a team of tech innovators building a hybrid Health Monitoring System for astronauts in microgravity. We are combining hardware sensors (using ESP32) to track real-time vitals and developing a custom software dashboard to visualize this data. We love coding, IoT, and space tech. We are ready to innovate!
summary:
OrbitLog is a real-time wireless astronaut biometric and spacesuit telemetry monitoring system developed by Team ORBIT LOG, consisting of Sreehari and Devanarayan, for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. The project aims to improve astronaut safety during Extravehicular Activities (EVA), commonly known as spacewalks, by continuously monitoring essential health parameters and spacesuit conditions. It uses wearable sensors, an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, wireless radio-frequency communication, and a Mission Control monitoring interface to detect possible medical emergencies and provide immediate alerts.

During spacewalks, astronauts work in an extremely challenging environment where there is no breathable atmosphere, gravity is almost absent, and temperature and pressure conditions are very different from those on Earth. Even a minor spacesuit malfunction or sudden change in an astronaut's health can become life-threatening. Problems such as abnormal heart rate, reduced blood oxygen levels, breathing difficulties, excessive physical stress, and changes in spacesuit pressure require continuous monitoring. ORBIT LOG addresses these challenges by collecting real-time biometric and pressure data and transmitting it wirelessly to a monitoring system.
details:
ORBIT LOG (OrbitLogic) – Astronaut Health & Spacesuit Telemetry Monitoring System

Project Overview

ORBIT LOG is a real-time wireless astronaut health and spacesuit telemetry monitoring system developed by Team ORBIT LOG (Sreehari and Devanarayan) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. The project aims to improve astronaut safety during Extravehicular Activities (EVA), commonly known as spacewalks, by continuously monitoring important physiological parameters and pressure-related changes.

Astronauts working in space face extreme environmental conditions, including microgravity, reduced spacesuit pressure, physical stress, and potential life-support system failures. These conditions can cause dangerous changes in heart rate, blood oxygen levels, and breathing patterns. ORBIT LOG is designed to detect these changes and communicate important health information to a Mission Control monitoring interface.

How Does It Work?

The system uses an ESP32-S3 microcontroller connected to three primary sensing components:

  • MAX30102: Monitors pulse-related signals and estimates blood oxygen saturation (SpO2).
  • V1706 Analog Pulse Sensor: Provides an additional pulse signal for backup heartbeat monitoring.
  • Square FSR Pressure Sensor: Detects chest pressure variations to estimate breathing patterns.

The sensors continuously collect data and transfer it to the ESP32-S3 for processing. The microcontroller prepares telemetry information approximately once per second and transmits it wirelessly using its built-in 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi capability.

The received information is displayed on a Mission Control laptop through a Serial Monitor and local monitoring dashboard. The system uses configured safety thresholds to identify potentially dangerous conditions.

For example:

  • Heart rate above 120 BPM triggers a high-heart-rate warning.
  • Blood oxygen saturation below 90% triggers a low-oxygen warning.
  • Normal monitored readings display SYSTEM SECURE – EVA NORMAL.

The proposed communication architecture is inspired by real space communication systems, including UHF, S-band, and NASA's Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System (TDRSS). These satellite communication stages represent the project's proposed future architecture; the current prototype demonstrates local wireless telemetry using ESP32-S3 Wi-Fi.

Benefits of the Project

  1. Continuous monitoring of important astronaut health parameters.
  2. Early identification of abnormal heart rate and oxygen saturation readings.
  3. Additional pulse monitoring through dual-sensor architecture.
  4. Breathing-pattern estimation using chest movement and pressure sensing.
  5. Wireless telemetry without depending on conventional terrestrial internet.
  6. Automated warnings that help Mission Control identify potential emergencies.
  7. A modular and expandable design that can support additional sensors in future versions.

Intended Impact

The primary goal of ORBIT LOG is to contribute to safer human space exploration by demonstrating how wearable sensors and wireless telemetry can support continuous astronaut health monitoring.

The project aims to help identify potential health emergencies earlier, improve awareness of an astronaut's physical condition, and provide useful information to Mission Control teams.

In the future, the concept could be expanded with additional sensors for body temperature, carbon dioxide levels, suit pressure, oxygen supply, and movement detection. Advanced data analysis could also help identify unusual health patterns.

Beyond space exploration, similar monitoring concepts could inspire applications in industrial safety, hazardous environments, emergency response, and remote health monitoring.

Tools, Hardware and Technologies Used

Our prototype uses the following technologies:

  • ESP32-S3 microcontroller (S3-N16R8 / HW678).
  • MAX30102 optical pulse oximeter.
  • V1706 analog pulse sensor.
  • Square Force Sensitive Resistor (FSR).
  • 10 kΩ resistor for the FSR voltage-divider circuit.
  • I2C communication protocol.
  • GPIO-based analog and digital sensor connections.
  • 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi wireless communication.
  • Serial Monitor at 115200 baud.
  • Local telemetry dashboard accessible through 192.168.4.1.

The hardware connections include MAX30102 SDA on GPIO 8, SCL on GPIO 9, V1706 analog output on GPIO 4, and FSR output on GPIO 5.

The ESP32-S3 firmware handles sensor acquisition, data processing, and wireless transmission. The project description does not specify a particular programming language or development IDE.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of ORBIT LOG is the integration of multiple health-monitoring sensors into a single wearable astronaut monitoring concept.

Instead of monitoring only one health parameter, the system combines heartbeat monitoring, oxygen saturation measurement, and breathing-related pressure sensing. The use of two pulse sensors introduces an additional monitoring channel, while the ESP32-S3 provides a compact processing and wireless communication platform.

Another innovative aspect is the combination of wearable biometric monitoring with a space-inspired RF telemetry architecture. The project connects astronaut health monitoring with the broader concept of spacecraft communication and Mission Control operations.

Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered several important factors while developing ORBIT LOG:

  • Astronaut safety and the importance of continuous health monitoring.
  • The extreme environmental conditions experienced during spacewalks.
  • The need for a compact and wearable electronic system.
  • Sensor accuracy, reliability, and redundancy.
  • Low-voltage sensor compatibility with the ESP32-S3.
  • Wireless communication without conventional internet infrastructure.
  • Fast transmission and understandable presentation of telemetry data.
  • Clear warning thresholds for identifying potentially dangerous readings.
  • Future scalability and integration with advanced space communication systems.

Conclusion

ORBIT LOG demonstrates how affordable microcontrollers, wearable sensors, and wireless communication technologies can be combined to create an astronaut health-monitoring prototype.

Our vision is to contribute to a future where astronauts can be monitored continuously and potential emergencies can be identified earlier. By combining biometric sensing, telemetry, and automated alerts, ORBIT LOG presents an innovative concept focused on making space exploration safer.

Team ORBIT LOG – Sreehari & Devanarayan
